newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Belgacom faces battle as EU deadline nears.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Belgacom faces battle as EU deadline nears.

text.p: With six months to go until Europe's telecommunications market is opened fully to competition, challengers to Belgium's partly-privatised monopoly provider Belgacom are lining up on its home market.

Belgium's telecoms regulator has so far granted licences to six groups to operate telecoms services, although they will not be able to compete in voice telephony until January 1 1998, the official European Union liberalisation deadline.
They are:

Telenet Vlaanderen, a joint venture between U.S. West Media Group and local partners including regional cable television groups and investment company GIMV; WorldCom, a joint venture between WorldCom and local cable television firm Coditel;
Hermes Railtel BV, a joint venture between 11 European railway companies and U.S. Global Telecommunication Systems;
SNCB/NMBS, the Belgian national railways company;
Brussels cable television networks Brutele and
Radio Public.

While the picture may look bleak for Belgacom and its industrial partners -- Ameritech, Tele Danmark and Singapore Telecom -- the competition is at present cherry-picking and not trying to compete in all service areas.

Only Telenet Vlaanderen, once it is fully operational next year, aims to challenge Belgacom's domestic voice monopoly, and then only in the northern, Dutch-speaking half of Belgium, where it plans to convert the region's cable TV infrastructure into a broadband communications network.
The Brussels cable companies are focusing on providing Internet access.
WorldCom is wiring only Brussels, where it hopes to capture a slice of corporate business and telecoms traffic generated by the capital's international institutions (the EU and NATO).
SNCB and Hermes are "carriers' carriers" -- selling capacity on the fibre optic cables that run along railway lines both to domestic (SNCB) and international (Hermes) operators.

Hermes at present has one link to the Netherlands, although connections to Britain and France are planned for the near future. The SNCB hopes to offer its domestic infrastructure to operators from October.
Belgacom says it is ready to meet the challengers and is fighting back. "We do our homework and see no reason to run away just because competition is coming," one official said.
A clock by the entrance to the company's headquarters reminds Belgacom staff each day how much time is left to prepare for liberalisation. It counts down in seconds.

Last week Belgacom announced plans to slash domestic prices from next March, about the time Telenet is due to start operations. It has also cut international call rates in the past year to meet competition from U.S.-based "call-back" services.
In compliance with EU laws that had to be implemented by July 1 Belgacom also published details of how much it will charge competitors to connect to its network.
The so-called "reference interconnection offer" must still be approved by the country's regulator. A decision is not likely until September. Already some competitors are crying foul.
"We are not very pleased. The average interconnection offer is one third higher than France Telecom's," Telenet spokesman Philippe Van Wassenhove told Reuters.
"We do not yet have full details, but it seems the whole market will have to pay for what has happened in the past, such as the problem of funding (Belgacom's) pensions," he added.

British Telecom, whose BT WorldWide unit is already offering data and private network services to multinational companies in Belgium, is among other operators waiting to examine the interconnection charges before taking a decision on whether to attack the market.

"We have not yet officially been informed of the offer but BT is planning to meet Belgacom shortly to start negotiations," BT Brussels representative David Smith said. He declined to comment on which market segments the British company was hoping to compete in.

Belgacom dismissed criticism of the proposed fees. "It's not surprising that when someone wants to buy something they want to get a better deal," a spokesman for the company's RTI (regulations, tariffs, interconnection) division told Reuters.

"The prices which have been published are...an offer which we have put on the table. We know every single operator has different requirements in terms of traffic. Since (the fees) are part of private contracts there will be variations," he said.
